days.title: Into the glen
days.body: Meet in Glasgow at nine, drive north and walk the last hour to camp. Dinner is on the deck.
days.meta: 6 km on foot · night under canvas
days.alt: A lit canvas tent on a wooden deck in a misty glen at dusk

days.title: The loch cabin
days.body: A boat takes the bags. You walk the shore path and reach the cabin as its lamps come on.
days.meta: 14 km on foot · night in a cabin
days.alt: A dark timber cabin with lit windows on a still loch at dusk

days.title: The western point
days.body: The most westerly headland of the mainland, grey seals below and nobody else on the path.
days.meta: 11 km on foot · 2 nights at the inn
days.alt: A grassy headland dropping into a grey sea under heavy cloud

days.title: The quiet bay
days.body: A slow day: the cliff path before breakfast, a swim for the brave and a long lunch in the dunes.
days.meta: 8 km on foot · free afternoon
days.alt: A still sea loch reflecting dark hills under cloud

days.title: Last light over the point
days.body: Ferry to Skye, then the lighthouse path. We carry supper up and stay until the sun is gone.
days.meta: 9 km on foot · ferry crossing
days.alt: Low sun breaking through cloud over a long valley

days.title: Last night by the fire
days.body: A boat into the loch under the Cuillin, a stove, a piper and the drive home in the morning.
days.meta: 5 km on foot · night in a dome
days.alt: A dome room with a stove and a wide window onto a loch

days.title: Up the valley
days.body: Meet at Dobbiaco station at two. A short walk to the first rifugio and a briefing over polenta.
days.meta: 4 km on foot · night in a rifugio

days.title: The lake before seven
days.body: We row at first light, before the car park fills, then climb to a hut above the water for lunch.
days.meta: 9 km on foot · 1 hour by boat
days.alt: Two travellers rowing a wooden boat on a green alpine lake under grey peaks

days.title: Across the plateau
days.body: A high, wide day on old shepherd tracks. Marmots, no road and a hut that makes its own cheese.
days.meta: 13 km on foot · night in a rifugio

days.title: The first pass
days.body: Up through larch to the pass and the wartime tunnels above it. A cable car spares the knees on the way down.
days.meta: 11 km on foot · cable car down

days.title: Five towers
days.body: A shorter day under the towers. Marco sets up a rope for anyone who wants to try the rock.
days.meta: 7 km on foot · free afternoon
days.alt: A small group walking a trail toward the Cinque Torri rock towers

days.title: The long pass
days.body: The biggest day of the week, started early. Lunch is on the grass at the top, with the coffee pot.
days.meta: 15 km on foot · night in a rifugio

days.title: The larch lake
days.body: Down to a small lake ringed with larch, and a swim if the sun is out. Last hut night, long dinner.
days.meta: 10 km on foot · night at the lake hut
days.alt: A mountain hut beside a still lake ringed with autumn larch

days.title: Down to Cortina
days.body: A two-hour descent to town, coffee in the square and the bus to the station by noon.
days.meta: 6 km on foot · ends at noon

days.title: Aboard at Sorong
days.body: Meet at the harbour at four. Cabins, a safety talk and the first dinner on deck as we leave port.
days.meta: By boat · night aboard
days.alt: A wooden phinisi at anchor with its lamps lit at dusk

days.title: The check dive
days.body: An easy reef to settle weights and buddies. Sari hands out the fish list at lunch.
days.meta: 2 dives · night aboard

days.title: The wall
days.body: A coral wall with more fish than you can count, and usually a turtle. The second dive rides the afternoon current.
days.meta: 2 dives · night aboard
days.alt: A diver beside a coral wall with a sea turtle in clear blue water

days.title: The village jetty
days.body: One dive under the jetty, then ashore. The children show you the school and beat you at football.
days.meta: 1 dive · afternoon ashore

days.title: The cleaning station
days.body: Kneel on the sand and wait. On most mornings the mantas come in to be cleaned and circle overhead.
days.meta: 2 dives · night aboard
days.alt: A manta ray gliding under a snorkeller in blue water

days.title: The lookout
days.body: No diving before lunch. A wooden stair to the view over the karst islands, then a drift dive on the way back.
days.meta: 320 steps · 1 dive
days.alt: Karst islands in a green lagoon seen from a wooden lookout

days.title: The hidden bay
days.body: Kayaks through the mangrove channels, a snorkel over soft coral and a night dive for those who want it.
days.meta: By kayak · night dive

days.title: The last reef
days.body: Two slow dives on the south side and a fire on the beach. Logbooks are signed after dinner.
days.meta: 2 dives · night aboard

days.title: Back to port
days.body: In harbour by eight. Breakfast aboard, then the transfer to the airport.
days.meta: Ends at 9:00 · transfer included

days.title: Meet on the wharf
days.body: Meet at three, walk the bay path and eat early. Everyone is still on another clock.
days.meta: 3 km on foot · night in Monterey

days.title: The cypress headland
days.body: Fog in the cypress at eight, sea lions below, and the headland to ourselves for an hour.
days.meta: 7 km on foot · night in Carmel
days.alt: Two walkers on a cliff path under cypress trees above a grey sea

days.title: Highway 1 at first light
days.body: On the road by six. Tomás stops at the turnouts with no sign, and we walk the bluff before the traffic.
days.meta: 40 km by road · 5 km on foot
days.alt: A coast road curving along sea cliffs toward a bridge in low cloud

days.title: Under the redwoods
days.body: A morning among the big trees along the river, an afternoon with nothing planned and cabins in the grove.
days.meta: 9 km on foot · night in a cabin

days.title: Dinner on the beach
days.body: Purple sand, the rock arch at sunset and a table set on the beach. Bring a jumper.
days.meta: 4 km on foot · dinner on the sand

days.title: The cove and the fall
days.body: Down through a tunnel to the old landing, then on to the waterfall that drops onto the sand.
days.meta: 6 km on foot · night in a cabin

days.title: The empty stretch
days.body: The road south has few houses and fewer cars. Condors if the wind is right, and elephant seals at the end.
days.meta: 95 km by road · night in Cambria

days.title: The last morning
days.body: Coffee by the harbour, a short paddle for anyone keen, and the van to the station by one.
days.meta: Ends at 13:00 · transfer included

days.title: Shoes off
days.body: A short flight from Malé, then the dhoni. Shoes go in a basket and stay there for a week.
days.meta: 20 minutes by air · night on the island
days.alt: A traveller sitting cross-legged on a wooden jetty at sunrise

days.title: The manta bay
days.body: Snorkel only, no tanks. When the plankton is in, the mantas feed in lines and you float above them.
days.meta: By dhoni · 2 snorkels
days.alt: A manta ray gliding under a snorkeller in blue water

days.title: A sandbank to ourselves
days.body: One umbrella, a cool box and a strip of sand that is gone at high tide. Lunch is grilled on the boat.
days.meta: By dhoni · a day on the sand
days.alt: A white sandbank with one umbrella in a turquoise lagoon, seen from above

days.title: The island that works
days.body: A morning with the boat builders and a lunch cooked by three sisters. Shoulders and knees are covered ashore.
days.meta: By dhoni · afternoon ashore

days.title: The reef edge
days.body: Two slow dives or snorkels along the drop. Turtles most days, a reef shark on some.
days.meta: 2 dives · night on the island

days.title: Back to the bay
days.body: A second visit for anyone who wants more mantas. Everyone else gets a hammock and a book.
days.meta: By dhoni · free afternoon

days.title: Shoes on
days.body: The basket comes back. A morning flight to Malé, in time for the evening departures.
days.meta: Ends at 11:00 · flight included

days.title: Cast off from Naoussa
days.body: Aboard at five. Cabins, a swim off the stern and dinner in the harbour.
days.meta: By boat · night in harbour

days.title: The first crossing
days.body: Two hours under sail to a bay with a single taverna. Whoever wants the helm gets it.
days.meta: 12 miles under sail · night at anchor
days.alt: A two-masted sailing yacht under way below an island headland at dusk

days.title: The empty island
days.body: Nobody lives here. A cove, a dig on the hill and our boat alone in the bay.
days.meta: 8 miles under sail · swim stop
days.alt: A cove with a small boat on a rocky island coast

days.title: Into Vathi
days.body: The longest sail of the week, then a round bay with potteries on the beach. Eleni's cousin cooks.
days.meta: 24 miles under sail · night in harbour
days.alt: A wooden fishing boat moored in a clear cove at golden hour

days.title: A day ashore
days.body: Legs need land. A bus up to Apollonia, the path down to Kastro and back to the boat for a swim.
days.meta: 6 km on foot · night in harbour
days.alt: A whitewashed island house with an arched door at golden hour

days.title: The white cliffs
days.body: A short hop to chalk cliffs and a village with more cats than cars.
days.meta: 14 miles under sail · night at anchor

days.title: The sea caves
days.body: Kleftiko can only be reached by water. We anchor early and swim through the arches before the day boats.
days.meta: 16 miles under sail · swim stop
days.alt: A turquoise rocky coast seen from above

days.title: Ashore at Adamas
days.body: Breakfast aboard, bags on the quay by ten, and the ferry or the small airport from there.
days.meta: Ends at 10:00 · on the quay
days.alt: A table for two on a terrace above a bay at dusk

days.title: Off the ferry
days.body: Eleni meets the afternoon boat. A short climb to stretch, rooms above the port and dinner on the sand.
days.meta: 3 km on foot · night in Kamares
days.alt: A wooden signpost on a stone path above a blue cove

days.title: Up to the villages
days.body: The old mule path climbs from the port to the white villages on the ridge. Lunch is at four.
days.meta: 9 km on foot · night in Apollonia
days.alt: A path along dry hills above a blue sea at golden hour

days.title: The walled village
days.body: Along the ridge and down to a village built as its own wall. Swim from the rocks under the chapel.
days.meta: 8 km on foot · night in Apollonia
days.alt: A whitewashed lane with flower pots and stone steps down to the sea

days.title: The monastery on the rock
days.body: A coast path past three coves to the white monastery on its rock. The sea is on your left all day.
days.meta: 11 km on foot · night in Faros

days.title: The potters' bay
days.body: A half day. One of the last potters lets you ruin a pot, and the afternoon is yours.
days.meta: 6 km on foot · free afternoon

days.title: Over the hill to Vathi
days.body: The quietest path of the week, with no road in sight, to a table at the water.
days.meta: 12 km on foot · night in Vathi
days.alt: A terrace table set for lunch above the sea

days.title: The boat home
days.body: A fishing boat takes us round the coast to the port, in time for the midday ferry.
days.meta: 40 minutes by boat · ends at noon

days.title: Off the sleeper
days.body: Meet the morning train. Kit check, spare gloves handed out and a short walk in through the pines.
days.meta: 5 km on foot · night in a bothy
days.alt: A stone bothy with lit windows among frosted birches

days.title: The river glen
days.body: Old pines, a frozen river and a bothy with the fire already lit. Calum cooks.
days.meta: 10 km on foot · night in a bothy
days.alt: A stone room with a stove and a lamp-lit bed

days.title: Above the cloud
days.body: If the weather allows, up to the plateau edge for the view. If not, the low path and more tea.
days.meta: 8 km on foot · 600 m of climb
days.alt: Morning cloud lying in the glens below dark hills

days.title: The frozen loch
days.body: A flat day round the loch and its island castle, then the last bothy and a dram.
days.meta: 9 km on foot · night in a bothy

days.title: Out by lunch
days.body: Out through the forest to a hot lunch in the village and the afternoon train south.
days.meta: 6 km on foot · ends at 14:00

days.title: Aboard the trawler
days.body: Meet on the quay at four. Six cabins, one long table and the first loch before dark.
days.meta: 8 miles by boat · night aboard
days.alt: A small trawler at anchor in a still sea loch under low cloud

days.title: Otters at breakfast
days.body: Anchor up late. The otters work the shore at low tide, and the skipper knows which rock.
days.meta: 12 miles by boat · walk ashore
days.alt: A still sea loch under heavy cloud with dark hills

days.title: The bird cliffs
days.body: Two hours across open water to cliffs full of puffins in season. Back in shelter by evening.
days.meta: 22 miles by boat · night at anchor

days.title: The long loch
days.body: Fourteen miles inland with hills on both sides. Kayaks go off the stern for the last hour.
days.meta: By boat and kayak · night aboard
days.alt: A long dark loch reflecting a low sky

days.title: An evening ashore
days.body: Legs on land. A walk to the lighthouse and supper in the island hall.
days.meta: 7 km on foot · night aboard

days.title: No road in
days.body: A loch you can only reach by sea. Mussels from the rocks, cooked on deck.
days.meta: 15 miles by boat · night at anchor
days.alt: An empty glen in mist with dark forest on both sides

days.title: Back round the point
days.body: An early start with the tide, and alongside by eleven for the ferry and the lunchtime flight.
days.meta: 20 miles by boat · ends at 11:00

tours.title: The Highland coast on foot
tours.alt: A lit canvas tent on a wooden deck in a misty highland glen at dusk
tours.description: Six days from glen to sea cliff with twelve travellers, a stove in every tent and a guide from Oban.
tours.included: Every night's bed: canvas, cabin, inn and dome; All meals from dinner on day one to breakfast on the last morning; Bags moved by boat and van; The ferry to Skye and the boat into Loch Coruisk; Your guide and a second leader
tours.excluded: Travel to Glasgow; Travel insurance; Drinks at the inn; Walking boots and waterproofs
tours.body:
This is a walking tour for people who walk at weekends, not for mountaineers. The longest day is fourteen kilometres on a shore path and the shortest is five. A boat or a van carries the bags, so you carry water, lunch and a jacket.

The pace is unhurried on purpose. We start after breakfast, stop when the light is good and reach each night's bed with time to sit outside before dinner. Day four is half free: the cliff path early, then nothing until supper unless you want it.

What makes it is where you sleep. Canvas with a stove in Glen Etive, a cabin on the loch, the inn at Ardnamurchan and a dome under the Cuillin. Calum has walked this coast since he was a boy and plans each day around the weather that morning. Bring waterproofs and expect to use them.

tours.title: Lakes and passes of the Dolomites
tours.alt: Two travellers rowing a wooden boat on a green alpine lake under grey peaks
tours.description: Row Lago di Braies before the day trippers, cross three passes on foot and sleep in family-run rifugios.
tours.included: Seven nights in family-run rifugios, in shared rooms; Breakfast and dinner every day, and picnic lunches; The rowing boat on Lago di Braies; One cable car; A certified alpine guide and a second leader; Bags moved by road on four days
tours.excluded: Travel to Dobbiaco and home from Cortina; Travel insurance with mountain cover; Drinks; A sheet sleeping bag for the huts
tours.body:
This is a hut-to-hut walk for people who are comfortable with six hours on their feet and a few hundred metres of climb before lunch. There is no climbing and no drop you cannot walk around. If you have done a long weekend in the hills with a rucksack, you are ready.

The days are honest: between four and fifteen kilometres, three passes, and one cable car down when the knees have earned it. One afternoon is free. Bags travel by road on four days. On the others you carry what you need for the night.

What makes it is the huts and the hour on the lake. Rifugios here are family houses with a kitchen, and Marco has known most of the families for twenty years. We row Lago di Braies at first light, when the water is flat and the car park is empty.

tours.title: A reef week in Raja Ampat
tours.alt: A diver beside a coral wall with a sea turtle in clear blue water
tours.description: Nine days on a wooden phinisi, two dives a day and a marine biologist on board.
tours.included: Eight nights aboard in a twin cabin; All meals, tea, coffee and water; Up to twelve guided dives with tanks and weights; Marine park fees; Airport transfers in Sorong; A marine biologist and two dive guides
tours.excluded: Flights to Sorong; Dive kit hire, $35 a day; Dive insurance, which is required; Tips for the crew
tours.body:
This is a dive trip for certified divers with at least twenty logged dives. Some sites have current, and you should be at ease with a drift and a safety stop in blue water. Non-divers are welcome and can snorkel every site but two.

The boat sets the pace. Two dives on most days, one before breakfast and one after lunch, with long hours in between for sleep, books and Sari's talks on deck. Days four and six are lighter, with time ashore.

What makes it is the reef and the person explaining it. Raja Ampat sits in the middle of the Coral Triangle, and one dive here can show two hundred kinds of fish. Sari has studied these reefs since university. You get her fish list on day two. By day eight most people have ticked a hundred and know which ones to leave alone.

tours.title: The Big Sur coast road
tours.alt: Two walkers on a cliff path under cypress trees above a grey sea
tours.description: Highway 1 at first light, cliff walks before the crowds and dinner on the beach.
tours.included: Seven nights: inns in Monterey, Carmel and Cambria, and cabins in the redwoods; Breakfast every day, five dinners and all picnic lunches; A twelve-seat van with a window for everyone; Park entry fees; Your guide, who also drives
tours.excluded: Flights to San Francisco or San José; Two dinners on your own; Travel insurance; Tips
tours.body:
This is a road trip for people who want the coast without the driving. It suits anyone who can walk two hours on a cliff path. There are no long hikes, and you can sit out any walk with a flask and the view.

The pace follows the light, not the map. The whole road is about a hundred and fifty kilometres, and we take eight days over it. We are out early, when the fog sits in the cypress and the turnouts are empty, and off the road by mid afternoon. Three nights are in the same redwood cabins, so you unpack once in the middle.

What makes it is Tomás. He drove this road for work before he guided on it, and he knows which turnouts have no sign and a path. One evening the table is set on the sand, and the van carries the jumpers.

tours.title: Sandbanks of Baa Atoll
tours.alt: A white sandbank with one umbrella in a turquoise lagoon, seen from above
tours.description: A week between sandbanks by dhoni, manta season in Hanifaru Bay and no shoes at all.
tours.included: Six nights in a family guesthouse on Dharavandhoo; All meals; The dhoni and its crew every day; Snorkel kit, and the permits and ranger fees for Hanifaru Bay; Flights between Malé and Dharavandhoo; A marine biologist as your guide
tours.excluded: Flights to Malé; Scuba dives, $60 each with a local centre; Travel insurance; Alcohol, which local islands do not serve
tours.body:
This is a week for swimmers, not only for divers. Hanifaru Bay is snorkel-only by law, so if you can float face down and breathe through a tube you can see everything the trip is built around. Children from ten are welcome with a parent.

The pace is slow and wet. One outing by dhoni most mornings, back for lunch, and the afternoons left open for a hammock or the house reef. Nothing starts before eight except the tide.

What makes it is the season and the stay. From May the plankton gathers in the bay and the mantas follow it in. We stay on a local island in a family guesthouse, not a resort, which is why the price is what it is and why shoulders stay covered in the village. Sari reads the tide tables each evening and picks the hour.

tours.title: The Cyclades by sailboat
tours.alt: A two-masted sailing yacht under way below an island headland at dusk
tours.description: Eight days under sail between five islands, swimming off the stern and eating where the fishermen eat.
tours.included: Seven nights aboard in a double or twin cabin; Breakfast and lunch aboard every day, and four dinners ashore; Skipper, fuel, harbour fees and bed linen; Snorkels and two paddleboards; Your guide
tours.excluded: Ferries or flights to Paros and home from Milos; Three dinners ashore; Travel insurance; Tips for the skipper
tours.body:
This is a sailing week for people who have never sailed, and for people who have and miss it. Nobody has to pull a rope. Anyone who wants to steer, trim a sail or learn the knots will be handed something within the hour.

The pace depends on the wind, which is the point. Most days are two to four hours under sail, a long swim stop, and a harbour or an anchorage by late afternoon. Day five is on land. If the meltemi blows hard we change the order of the islands, not the number.

What makes it is the size of the boat. Fifteen metres, four guest cabins and a keel shallow enough for coves the ferries and day boats cannot use. Eleni eats where the fishermen eat, and on two nights that is a table with no menu.

tours.title: The Aegean coast path
tours.alt: A path along dry hills above a blue sea at golden hour
tours.description: Old mule paths from village to village, a swim at the end of each day and a table by the water.
tours.included: Six nights in family-run rooms, each with its own bathroom; Breakfast every day and lunch at the end of each walk; Bags moved between villages; The boat back to Kamares; Your guide
tours.excluded: The ferry to Sifnos; Dinners, about $25 with wine; Travel insurance; Walking poles
tours.body:
This is a walking week for people who like a path more than a summit. Sifnos is small, and the old mule tracks between its villages are paved in stone, walled on both sides and shaded for some of the way. If you can walk four hours with stops, you can do all of it.

The pace is set by the heat and by lunch. We start at eight, walk until one or two, swim, and sit down to eat at four as the island does. Dinners are your own, and Eleni will tell you whose table has room. Day five is a half day.

What makes it is that it is one island, done properly. You are never in a vehicle between the first ferry and the last boat. By Thursday the baker knows your order.

tours.title: Winter bothies of the Cairngorms
tours.alt: A stone bothy with lit windows among frosted birches
tours.description: Five short winter days between stone bothies, with a fire lit before you arrive.
tours.included: Four nights in stone bothies, with sleeping bags and mats; All meals, cooked on the stove; Winter kit on loan: an insulated jacket, microspikes and a head torch; Transfers from and to Aviemore station; Two guides with winter mountain training
tours.excluded: The train to Aviemore; Walking boots; Travel insurance; Drinks in the village on the last day
tours.body:
This is a short winter trip for people who are curious about bothies and not sure about the cold. You need to be able to walk three hours on snow or frozen ground with a pack of about eight kilos. You do not need winter skills. We lend the kit and show you how to use it.

The days are short because the light is. We walk from nine to about two and reach the bothy with the fire already lit. The evening is soup, cards and an early night. Day three goes high only if the weather allows it.

What makes it is the bothy. No power, no signal, one stove and a room that is warm by five. A second guide goes ahead with the food and the wood, so you arrive to a lit window. Bring a book you can read by torch.

tours.title: Sea lochs of the Hebrides
tours.alt: A small trawler at anchor in a still sea loch under low cloud
tours.description: A converted trawler, seven sea lochs, otters at breakfast and a skipper from Stornoway.
tours.included: Six nights aboard in a twin cabin; All meals, cooked in the galley; Fuel, harbour dues and bed linen; Kayaks and waterproofs on loan; Your guide and a crew of two
tours.excluded: Travel to Stornoway; Travel insurance; Drinks from the honesty shelf; Sea-sickness tablets, which we advise
tours.body:
This is a slow week on a boat for people who would rather watch a shoreline than tick off sights. No sailing skill is asked for. You need to be steady on a ladder and happy in a small cabin.

The pace is the tide's. We move for two or three hours most days, anchor in a different sea loch each night and go ashore by dinghy when there is something to walk to. One crossing, to the Shiant Isles, is open water and can be lumpy. If the forecast is poor we stay inside, and nobody minds.

What makes it is the trawler and the people on her. She fished out of Stornoway for thirty years before the refit, and the skipper worked on her as a boy. Twelve berths, one long table and a wheelhouse you are welcome in. Otters most mornings. Signal almost never.

guides.name: Calum MacRae
guides.description: Grew up on a croft above the Sound of Mull and has walked every glen we use, most of them in the rain.
guides.alt: Calum MacRae, a bearded man in an oatmeal sweater
guides.body:
Calum grew up on a croft above the Sound of Mull, the youngest of four, and left at eighteen to work on fishing boats out of Oban. He came back to the hills in his thirties, trained as a mountain leader and joined Landfall in its first year. He has led most of our Scottish departures since, in every month of the year.

He plans by the weather, not the brochure. If the cloud is down on the ridge he will take you along the shore instead and tell you why it is the better day. He cooks on the bothy trips, carries a spare pair of gloves for whoever forgot theirs and plays the whistle badly when asked. He lives in Oban with a collie called Skerry.

guides.name: Eleni Vardaki
guides.description: Her grandmother ran the bakery in Apollonia. She knows which path is open and whose table has room.
guides.alt: Eleni Vardaki in a rust coat on a cobbled street
guides.body:
Eleni was born in Apollonia, on Sifnos, where her grandmother ran the village bakery for forty years. She studied archaeology in Athens, worked two summers on a dig on Despotiko and came home when she realised she liked the walk to the site more than the trench.

She has guided for Landfall since 2013 and leads both of our Greek tours: the walking week on Sifnos and the sailing week through the western Cyclades. She knows which paths were cleared this spring, which chapel has the key under the stone and whose kitchen is open on a Monday. She will order for the table unless you stop her. In winter she presses olives with her father and mends the stone walls along the paths we use.

guides.name: Marco De Luca
guides.description: A certified alpine guide for twenty-six years. He still carries the coffee pot.
guides.alt: Marco De Luca, a grey-bearded man with a climbing rope on a Dolomites trail
guides.body:
Marco was born in Cortina and has been a certified alpine guide for twenty-six years. Before Landfall he spent a decade leading climbers on the big walls of the Dolomites, then decided he preferred the people who walk between the huts and stop to look.

He joined us in 2011 and built the lakes and passes route himself, hut by hut, mostly by asking the families who run them what they wished visitors knew. He speaks Ladin with the hut keepers and switches without noticing. He carries a moka pot and a small stove in his pack and makes coffee at the top of every pass, whatever the weather. On the free afternoon he sets up a rope under the Cinque Torri for anyone who wants to try the rock.

guides.name: Sari Wulandari
guides.description: Marine biologist first, guide second. She will name every fish and tell you which ones to leave alone.
guides.alt: Sari Wulandari on a dive boat with a mask pushed up on her head
guides.body:
Sari trained as a marine biologist in Manado and spent four years counting fish on survey lines in the Dampier Strait before she led her first dive group. She joined Landfall in 2017. She still sends her counts to the university each season, and guests are welcome to help.

She leads our two reef trips. From October to April she is on the phinisi in Raja Ampat. From May she moves to Baa Atoll in the Maldives for the manta season, where the work is done with a snorkel and a tide table. On both she hands out a fish list on the second day and gives a short talk most evenings. Her one rule is simple: look as long as you like, touch nothing.

guides.name: Tomás Reyes
guides.description: Drove Highway 1 as a delivery driver before he guided on it. Knows every turnout worth the stop.
guides.alt: Tomás Reyes leaning on his van above the coast road
guides.body:
Tomás grew up in Carmel and spent six years driving a delivery van along Highway 1, from Monterey to the last ranch before San Simeon. He learned the road by its gates and its turnouts, and the people by what they ordered.

He started guiding for Landfall in 2019. He drives the van himself, which means the stops are his: a bluff with no sign, a bakery that sells out by nine, a bend where condors ride the wind on a clear afternoon. He is a patient birder and a fast cook, and he sets the table for the beach dinner while the group walks down to the arch. He will not promise you a condor. He will tell you his count for the season.

destinations.name: Scotland
destinations.description: Glens, sea lochs and stone bothies, on foot and by boat.
destinations.season: May to September, and deep winter
destinations.alt: A lit dome tent in a highland glen at dusk, a loch behind
destinations.body:
We run three tours in Scotland and all of them start north of the Highland line. The west coast is for walking between glens and sea cliffs in the long light of May and June. The Outer Hebrides are for the boat, when the sea lochs are calm and the otters have young. The Cairngorms are for January, when the bothies are empty and the snow is firm.

The weather is part of it. It changes four times a day, and the guides plan each morning around it. Midges arrive in late June on the west coast, which is why our walking dates pause in July and start again in September. Bring waterproofs whatever the month.
destinations.facts: Best months: May, June, September and January; Flight from Lisbon: 3 h 10 to Edinburgh; Pace: Easy to moderate, 5 to 14 km a day; Sleep: Canvas, cabins, bothies and a trawler

destinations.name: Greece
destinations.description: Island paths, coves you reach by sail and long tables by the water.
destinations.alt: A walled coastal town of terracotta roofs above a blue sea
destinations.body:
Our two Greek tours share one island and one guide. Sifnos sits in the western Cyclades, away from the big ferry routes, and Eleni grew up above its bakery. The walking week stays on the island and crosses it on stone mule paths. The sailing week starts in Paros, reaches Sifnos on day four and ends in the sea caves of Milos.

We go in May, June and September. July and August are hot, crowded and windy, and the paths are no pleasure at noon. In the months we choose, the sea is warm enough to swim every day and the tavernas still have time to talk. Lunch is at four. Plan around it.
destinations.facts: Best months: May, June and September; Flight from Lisbon: 4 h to Athens, then a ferry; Pace: Easy, with a swim every day; Sleep: Family rooms or a cabin aboard

destinations.name: Italy
destinations.description: The high lakes and passes of the Dolomites, hut to hut.
destinations.alt: Two travellers rowing on a green alpine lake
destinations.body:
In Italy we do one thing: the Dolomites, on foot, from hut to hut. The range is in the far north-east, closer to Innsbruck than to Rome, and the valleys speak Italian, German and Ladin. The paths are old and well marked, the huts are family houses with proper kitchens, and the rock turns pink for ten minutes at the end of a clear day.

The season is short. The high passes hold snow into June and the huts close in early October. September is the month we like most: settled weather, larch beginning to turn and room at the tables. Marco has guided here for twenty-six years and still carries the coffee pot to the top of every pass.
destinations.facts: Best months: Late June to September; Flight from Lisbon: 3 h to Venice, then 2 h by road; Pace: Moderate, 4 to 15 km a day; Sleep: Family-run rifugios

destinations.name: Indonesia
destinations.description: Raja Ampat by wooden phinisi, two dives a day.
destinations.alt: A diver beside a coral wall with a sea turtle
destinations.body:
Raja Ampat is a scatter of about fifteen hundred islands off the western tip of New Guinea. Getting there takes two flights and a patient day. That distance is why the reefs look the way they do. There is no large town on the islands, and only a few boats work the strait.

We go by phinisi, a wooden two-master built in Sulawesi, with eight cabins and a dive deck. The season runs from October to April, when the sea is flat and the water clear. Sari Wulandari leads every departure. She trained as a marine biologist in Manado and treats each dive as a field class, with a fish list and a quiet rule about what not to touch.
destinations.facts: Best months: October to April; Flight from Lisbon: About 24 h to Sorong, with two stops; Pace: Two dives a day and long rests; Sleep: A twin cabin aboard

destinations.name: Maldives
destinations.description: Sandbanks, manta season and a week without shoes.
destinations.alt: A white sandbank in a turquoise lagoon from above
destinations.body:
Most people see the Maldives from a resort jetty. We stay on Dharavandhoo, a local island in Baa Atoll with a school, a mosque, a football pitch and a handful of family guesthouses. The atoll is a protected biosphere reserve, and Hanifaru Bay inside it is the reason to come.

When the tide and the plankton line up, manta rays feed in the bay in long chains, and you float above them with a mask and a snorkel. Tanks are not allowed. Between visits there are sandbanks that appear at low tide, a reef with turtles a short swim from the beach, and very little else to do. Local islands serve no alcohol, and dress is modest in the village. Nobody wears shoes.
destinations.facts: Best months: May to November for mantas, November to April for calm seas; Flight from Lisbon: About 13 h to Malé, with one stop; Pace: Slow, one outing a day; Sleep: A family guesthouse

destinations.name: California
destinations.description: The Big Sur coast road, cliff walks and redwood nights.
destinations.alt: Cypress trees on a foggy sea cliff above the surf
destinations.body:
Our Californian tour covers one road: Highway 1 between Monterey and Morro Bay, the stretch known as Big Sur. It is about a hundred and fifty kilometres of cliffs, redwood canyons and very few buildings. People drive it in a day. We take eight.

Spring is the time. From March to June the hills are green, the wildflowers are out and the fog burns off by ten. Later in the year the road fills and the grass turns gold and dry. Slides sometimes close a section in winter, and Tomás checks the road each week before a departure. He grew up in Carmel, delivered along this road for six years and has an opinion about every turnout.
destinations.facts: Best months: March to June; Flight from Lisbon: About 14 h to San Francisco, with one stop; Pace: Easy, short cliff walks; Sleep: Inns and redwood cabins

posts.title: What a night in a bothy is actually like
posts.description: No power, one stove and the best sleep of the year. A plain account for people who have never tried it.
posts.author: Calum MacRae
posts.alt: A stone room with a stove and a lamp-lit bed
posts.body:
A bothy is a stone hut in the hills that nobody owns in the way you own a house. The door is not locked. There is a fireplace or a stove, a sleeping platform, sometimes a table. That is the whole list.

People ask me what it is like before they book the winter trip. This is the plain version.

## Arriving

You walk in. There is no road to any of the bothies we use, and the shortest approach is an hour and a half. In January the light goes at four, so we aim to be at the door by two.

On our trips the second guide has gone ahead with the wood and the food. You come round the last bend and there is a lit window and smoke. People go quiet at that point. I still do.

## The evening

Boots off at the door. The room is warm near the stove and cold by the far wall, and you learn within ten minutes where to sit. Supper is soup, then something heavy, then tea. There is no signal, so nobody looks at a phone after the first hour.

> The first night, people talk until ten. The second night they are asleep by half past eight, and they are happier for it.

We play cards. Someone always reads aloud from the bothy book, where walkers have left notes for fifty years.

## The night

You sleep on a wooden platform on a thick mat, in a bag rated well below zero. It is dark in a way most people have forgotten. If you go outside at midnight, and you should, the stars are close and the cold catches in your nose.

In the morning the stove is lit again before you are up. Porridge, sweep the floor, carry out everything you carried in. Then the door is pulled shut for whoever comes next.

posts.title: The table at the end of the path
posts.description: Why every walking day in Greece ends with lunch at four, and what to order when it does.
posts.author: Eleni Vardaki
posts.alt: A basket of fruit on a stone table above the sea
posts.body:
On the first day of every walking week somebody asks me when lunch is. I say four. They laugh, and at one o'clock they stop laughing.

## Why four

It is not a trick. On the islands the working day used to end when the heat made work foolish. People ate their main meal then, in the shade, and slept after it. The paths we walk were built for that day. They run from a village to a field, a chapel or a cove, and they take a morning.

So we walk the morning. We start at eight with coffee and a piece of bread, carry fruit and water, and reach the sea by one or two. Then we swim. Hunger after a swim is a different thing from hunger at a desk.

> My grandmother said a table by the sea needs three things: shade, bread and nobody looking at the time.

## What to order

Let the kitchen decide the fish. Ask what came in that morning and take it grilled, with lemon and nothing else.

Order chickpeas if it is Sunday. On Sifnos they go into the wood oven on Saturday night in a clay pot and come out at noon. Order the caper salad anywhere, and the small fried cheese pies when you see them.

Order less than you think. Plates are for the table, not for one person, and more will arrive whether you ask or not.

## After

Nobody walks after lunch. The bags have gone ahead. You take a nap, or the slow road back through the village when the light turns. Dinner, if you want one, is at nine and it is small.

By the fourth day most guests have stopped asking the time. That is when I know the week is working.

posts.title: When to go where: our calendar, month by month
posts.description: Twelve months, six countries and the two weeks in each when the place is at its best.
posts.author: Landfall
posts.alt: A turquoise rocky coast seen from above
posts.body:
We run tours in six countries and we do not run any of them all year. Each has a few weeks when the weather, the light and the crowds line up. This is how the year looks from our planning wall.

## Winter and spring

January and February belong to the Cairngorms. The snow is firm, the bothies are empty and the days are short enough that nobody minds an early night. It is also the calm season in Raja Ampat, where the phinisi sails from October to April.

March to early June is Big Sur. The hills are green, the fog lifts by ten and Highway 1 is quiet. In May the west coast of Scotland opens, before the midges and with light until eleven.

> If you can travel in only one month, make it May. Four of our six countries are open, and none of them is crowded.

## Summer

From late May the mantas gather in Baa Atoll, and the Hebrides are at their calmest for the boat. June is for Greece: warm sea, open paths, room at the table. We stop in July and August, when the islands are hot and full.

The Dolomites start in late June, once the passes are clear of snow, and the huts stay open into early October.

## Autumn

September is the second spring. Greece again, the Highland coast again, and the Dolomites with the larch turning. In October the boat goes back to Raja Ampat and the year starts over.

A few rules of thumb. Book winter bothies by October and summer boats by February, because both are small. Ask us about the week either side of a school holiday. And if your dates are fixed, tell us the dates first and the place second. There is nearly always somewhere good to go.

posts.title: What to pack for a walking week
posts.description: One day pack, two pairs of socks a day and nothing made of cotton. The list our guides send their own families.
posts.author: Calum MacRae
posts.alt: A path along dry hills above a blue sea at golden hour
posts.body:
Every walking tour we run moves your main bag for you. That changes what packing means. You are not choosing what you can carry for a week. You are choosing what you want on your back for five hours and what can wait in the van.

## On your back

A day pack of twenty to twenty-five litres with a hip belt. Inside it: a waterproof jacket, whatever the forecast says. A warm layer. Water, at least a litre and a half. Lunch, which we hand out at breakfast. Sun cream and a hat. A small dry bag for your phone.

That is all. If the pack weighs more than five kilos, something in it belongs in the other bag.

## On your feet

Boots or trail shoes you have already walked fifty kilometres in. This matters more than anything else on the list. New boots are the main reason people sit out a day.

Two pairs of socks for each walking day, wool or a wool mix. Change at lunch. It sounds fussy, and it is the difference between a blister on day three and none.

> Nobody has ever told me they wished they had brought a third pair of trousers. Plenty have wished for a second pair of dry socks.

## What to leave

Cotton, in any layer that touches skin. It holds water and stays cold. Jeans. A full wash bag. More than one book. An umbrella, unless you are going to Greece, where it makes a good sunshade.

Leave the drone. Leave the laptop if you can bear to.

For Scotland, add a midge net from late May and waterproof trousers all year. For the Dolomites, a sheet sleeping bag for the huts. For Greece, swimming things in the day pack, always, because the path ends at the sea.

posts.title: Your first week on a sailing boat
posts.description: Small cabins, bare feet and a toilet with instructions. A plain guide for people who have never slept afloat.
posts.author: Eleni Vardaki
posts.alt: A two-masted sailing yacht under way below an island headland at dusk
posts.body:
Half the people who join the Cyclades week have never slept on a boat. They ask the same five questions on the quay, so here are the answers before you pack.

## The boat is small, and that is fine

Your cabin is a bed with a door. There is room to stand in part of it and a shelf for a soft bag. Hard suitcases do not fit anywhere, so please do not bring one.

You will not be in the cabin much. Life is on deck and in the cockpit, under the shade, with your feet up. By the second day people leave their shoes in a basket and forget them.

The toilet has a pump and a short list of rules. The skipper explains it once, with a straight face. Listen.

## You do not have to do anything

Nobody has to pull a rope. If you want to, you will be shown how to steer, how to take in a sail and how to tie the three knots that hold everything on a boat.

> By Wednesday someone who had never sailed is at the helm, and the skipper is asleep with one eye open.

## Feeling ill

Some people do, on the first long crossing, for an hour or two. Stay on deck, look at the horizon and eat something dry. Take a tablet the night before if you know you are prone. It passes, and it rarely comes back after day two.

A few last things. Water aboard is limited, so showers are short and mostly off the stern in the sea. Bring a hat with a strap. Bring less than you think. And when the anchor goes down in an empty bay at five in the afternoon, be the first one in.

posts.title: Why we stop at twelve travellers
posts.description: A coach holds fifty. Our groups end at twelve. The reasons are a table, a van and a bothy floor.
posts.author: Landfall
posts.alt: A long timber room with lamps and windows onto a loch
posts.body:
Every tour on this site has the same number at the top: twelve travellers at most. People ask whether that is a marketing line. It is closer to a piece of arithmetic.

## What twelve fits

Twelve people fit around one table. That sounds small, and it decides most of a trip. At one table there is one conversation, or two, and nobody eats with their back to the group. At thirteen you need a second table, and the group quietly becomes two groups.

Twelve fit in one van with a window each. Twelve fit on the sleeping platform of the bothies we use, with the two guides by the door. The trawler in the Hebrides has twelve berths. The family rooms on Sifnos come to twelve beds if we take the whole house.

## What it costs

A smaller group costs more per person. The guide's wage, the van and the boat are split twelve ways instead of forty. We would rather say that plainly than hide it. It is the main reason our prices are what they are.

> A guide can learn twelve names by the first lunch. After that it is a group of people, not a headcount.

It also means some departures fill quickly, and we do not add a second van when they do. We add a second date.

## What it changes

With twelve, the plan can bend. If one person is slow on a climb, the group waits and nobody is late for anything. If the weather turns, we can change the day over breakfast, because twelve people can be told in one sentence.

Sometimes a tour runs with five or six. We do not cancel for small numbers once two people have booked. Those are often the departures guests write to us about afterwards.
